content.value: Transform boolean expressions using De Morgan’s laws and comparison complements; verify equivalence with truth tables and boundary tests.

Two boolean expressions are equivalent when they produce the same result for every allowed assignment of their inputs. Use a truth table for a small number of boolean variables and boundary tests for numeric comparisons. Examples can disprove equivalence, but one matching example does not prove it.

De Morgan’s laws move a negation across a compound expression: negate each operand and exchange AND with OR. Thus !(a && b) becomes !a || !b, and !(a || b) becomes !a && !b. Negating a comparison also changes its boundary: the complement of < is >=, and the complement of > is <=. Double negation restores the original condition.

outside and sameOutside agree. At x = 10 or 20 they are both false; at 9 or 21 they are true. Simply negating both comparisons while keeping AND would require x < 10 and x > 20 simultaneously, which cannot happen.

Parentheses matter when applying negation to an entire expression. Do not drop the equality boundary. Boolean equivalence does not justify moving unsafe method calls ahead of the checks that protect them.
Rewrite !(score < 0 || score > 100). Answer: score >= 0 && score <= 100. Explain why both boundaries are allowed and test -1, 0, 100, and 101.
